opus-5.5.text:
I think what drew me in is a mismatch that shows up when you train a small model by imitating a big one. In standard distillation, the student learns from sequences the teacher generated. At inference time, though, the student is generating its own text. It makes small mistakes, drifts into states the teacher never visited, and has no training signal for recovering from them. That's the classic exposure bias problem, the same one people ran into with imitation learning in robotics years ago.

On-policy distillation flips this around. The student generates its own outputs, and the teacher gives feedback on those outputs, token by token. So the student learns in exactly the distribution it will face when deployed, including its own errors. That's essentially the DAgger insight from imitation learning, carried over to language models. In our work on generalized knowledge distillation, we found this gave consistent gains on things like summarization, translation, and reasoning, compared with training only on teacher samples.

The second thing I find compelling is that it sits in a nice middle ground between supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. RL is on-policy too, but the reward is sparse. You might get one bit of signal at the end of a long reasoning chain. With on-policy distillation you get a dense signal: the teacher tells you, at every token, how it would have distributed probability. That's much more sample-efficient, and you can mix the two. You can add an RL objective for the task reward and use the distillation term to keep the student close to a strong teacher.

It's also flexible in which divergence you optimize. Forward KL tends to be mode-covering, so the student spreads its probability mass. Reverse KL is mode-seeking, so the student commits to the high-probability behaviors of the teacher. For a small model with limited capacity, being mode-seeking is often what you actually want. You'd rather it do a few things very well than smear itself thin trying to imitate everything.

Practically, as people deploy smaller models on devices or at lower cost, getting the most out of a fixed-size student matters a lot. On-policy distillation is one of the cleanest ways I know to close that gap. It's conceptually simple and easy to implement on top of existing RL infrastructure, so it's been satisfying to see it pick up in practice.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the thing that really grabbed me about on-policy distillation is that it fixes a mismatch that's been bugging me for a long time. The way distillation has traditionally worked for language models is you take the teacher, you generate a bunch of outputs from it, and you train the student with supervised learning on those outputs. That's sequence-level knowledge distillation, and it works, but there's a subtle problem: the student is only ever trained on the teacher's distribution. It never sees its own mistakes.

And then at test time, the student is generating autoregressively, so it's sampling from its own distribution, and the moment it drifts a little bit off the teacher's trajectory, it's in a state it has never been trained on. The errors compound. This is the same exposure bias story people have been talking about in sequence models for years, but distillation made it worse in a sense because you're handing the student this very clean, polished teacher data and then asking it to behave in a completely different regime.

On-policy distillation flips that. You sample from the student, and then you ask the teacher, token by token, what would you have done here? So the student gets dense feedback on its own trajectories, including the states it actually ends up in when it messes up. You're matching the teacher's distribution exactly where the student lives, not where the teacher lives.

What I find compelling about that is twofold. One is just that it's the right objective in a principled sense. If what you care about is how the student behaves when it's deployed, you should be training it on the states it visits when deployed. The other thing, which I think is underappreciated, is how it relates to RL. On-policy distillation is basically RL with a very dense, very informative reward. Instead of a single scalar at the end of the sequence saying this was right or wrong, you get a per-token signal from the teacher saying here's how surprised I am by what you did. So you get the on-policy benefits of RL, where the model learns from its own mistakes, but with vastly more signal per sample. That makes it much more compute efficient than doing RL from scratch, and it tends to be more stable too.

The other reason I keep coming back to it is practical. The large models we train now are extremely expensive to serve, and the whole game is getting a lot of that capability into something small. If you have a strong teacher that can be a verifier of reasoning, a judge of style, a pretty good proxy for a reward model, then on-policy distillation becomes a general-purpose tool. You can use it to recover capabilities after fine-tuning, to transfer reasoning behavior into smaller models, to personalize. It's a surprisingly simple idea that keeps turning out to be useful in a lot of places, and that's usually the mark of something that's actually right.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that you train the student on the kinds of outputs it actually produces. In standard distillation, you might give a smaller model responses generated by a stronger teacher. But when the student generates at inference time, it can take a different path, and suddenly it’s in a context that the teacher’s examples didn’t cover.

With on-policy distillation, you let the student generate and then ask the teacher to provide feedback on those contexts. So the learning signal is targeted at the student’s own behavior—where it’s uncertain or making mistakes. That’s particularly appealing for language models because generation is sequential: one mistake can change the context for everything that follows.

The tradeoff is that you need student rollouts during training, which adds cost. But you get a much closer match between the situations the model learns from and the situations it encounters when you actually use it.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that the student gets to learn on the kinds of outputs it actually produces. In standard distillation, you typically train on responses generated by a larger teacher. But at inference time, the student is conditioning on its own generations, and those can look quite different. A small mistake can put it in a context that it never saw during training.

With on-policy distillation, you sample from the student and ask the teacher to provide supervision along those trajectories. So the teacher is giving feedback precisely where the student needs it, including in situations where it’s already gone a little off track.

And with language models, you have this really useful source of feedback: the teacher’s distribution over the next token. That gives you much richer information than just a scalar reward. You can use that to transfer capabilities while training on a distribution that’s closer to what the student will encounter when you actually deploy it.
